skills.name: Adding within 20 with Strategies
skills.target: I can add two numbers within 20 in my head using strategies such as making a ten, doubles, and doubles plus one.
skills.misconception: Counting on from the first number and including that number (8 + 5 → 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 = 12).
skills.howToAddress: Count on from the next number with fingers or a number line, then teach make-a-ten with ten frames so counting is not needed.

skills.name: Subtracting within 20 with Strategies
skills.target: I can subtract within 20 in my head by thinking addition, counting back, or going back through ten.
skills.misconception: Subtracting the smaller digit from the larger one (14 − 6 → 6 − 4 = 2 → 12), or counting back and including the start number.
skills.howToAddress: Ask “What do I add to 6 to make 14?” and model the jump back to 10 and then the rest on a number line.

skills.name: Related Facts and Fact Families
skills.target: I can use an addition fact to find related addition and subtraction facts in the same fact family.
skills.misconception: Thinking the order of numbers can change in a subtraction fact (14 − 6 = 8 → 6 − 14 = 8).
skills.howToAddress: Build the fact family with a part-part-whole mat; the whole is always first in a subtraction fact.

skills.name: Missing Numbers in Equations within 20
skills.target: I can find the missing number in an addition or subtraction equation within 20 and tell if an equation is true.
skills.misconception: Thinking the equal sign means “write the answer next” (7 + ___ = 15 → 22).
skills.howToAddress: Read = as “is the same as” and check both sides with cubes or a balance picture.

units.name: Odd and Even Numbers and Arrays

skills.name: Odd and Even Numbers
skills.target: I can tell whether a group of up to 20 objects is odd or even by making pairs or counting by 2s.
skills.misconception: Looking at the tens digit instead of the ones digit, or thinking an odd number of objects can be put in pairs.
skills.howToAddress: Pair the objects; if one is left over, the number is odd. Then connect to the ones digit 0, 2, 4, 6, 8.

skills.name: Even Numbers as Doubles
skills.target: I can write an even number as the sum of two equal addends, such as 14 = 7 + 7.
skills.misconception: Writing two addends that are not equal (14 = 10 + 4), or trying to write an odd number as a double.
skills.howToAddress: Split the objects into two equal rows and check that every object has a partner.

skills.name: Arrays and Repeated Addition
skills.target: I can find the total in an array with up to 5 rows and 5 columns and write an addition equation with equal addends.
skills.misconception: Adding the number of rows and the number of columns (3 rows of 4 → 7).
skills.howToAddress: Circle each row, say how many are in it, and add the same number once for every row.

skills.name: Array Word Problems
skills.target: I can solve word problems about objects in rows and columns by drawing an array and writing an equation.
skills.misconception: Adding the two numbers in the story instead of adding the row number again and again.
skills.howToAddress: Draw the rows with dots, then write the row amount once for each row before adding.

skills.name: A Hundred Is Ten Tens
skills.target: I can explain that 100 is the same as ten tens and trade between tens and hundreds.
skills.misconception: Thinking 10 tens is 10 or 1,000, or not seeing a hundred flat as made of tens.
skills.howToAddress: Stack ten tens rods on a hundred flat and count by tens to 100.

skills.name: Hundreds, Tens, and Ones
skills.target: I can tell how many hundreds, tens, and ones are in a three-digit number and the value of each digit.
skills.misconception: Giving the digit instead of its value (the 4 in 249 is worth 4), or ignoring a zero (706 read as 76).
skills.howToAddress: Use base-ten blocks and a place-value chart; say the value aloud (“4 tens is 40”).

skills.name: Counting Hundreds
skills.target: I can tell that 100, 200, … 900 are one to nine hundreds with 0 tens and 0 ones.
skills.misconception: Writing 5 hundreds as 5 or 5,000, or 500 as “50 tens and 0 hundreds” without seeing both are true.
skills.howToAddress: Count hundred flats by 100s and write the number with zeros in the tens and ones places.

skills.name: Numerals, Number Names, and Expanded Form
skills.target: I can read and write numbers to 1,000 as numerals, in words, and in expanded form.
skills.misconception: Writing what is heard (“four hundred six” → 4006), or leaving out a zero place (400 + 6 → 46).
skills.howToAddress: Build the number with blocks first, then fill a place-value chart before writing it.

skills.name: Counting within 1,000
skills.target: I can count forward and backward within 1,000, including across tens and hundreds.
skills.misconception: Getting stuck when the count crosses a hundred (198, 199, 1,000) or a ten (409, 4,010).
skills.howToAddress: Count with base-ten blocks and trade; use a 1–1,000 number line and say the hundreds aloud.

skills.name: Skip Counting by 5s, 10s, and 100s
skills.target: I can skip count by 5s, 10s, and 100s from any starting number and continue the pattern.
skills.misconception: Switching to counting by 1s or by 10s partway through, especially across a hundred.
skills.howToAddress: Name which digit changes for each jump (ones for 5s, tens for 10s, hundreds for 100s) and check it.

skills.name: Comparing Three-Digit Numbers
skills.target: I can compare two three-digit numbers using hundreds, tens, and ones and record it with >, =, or <.
skills.misconception: Comparing digit by digit from the ones place, or thinking a number with bigger digits anywhere is greater (189 > 201).
skills.howToAddress: Start with the hundreds; only look at the tens when the hundreds are equal. Read the symbol from left to right.

skills.name: Adding and Subtracting 10 and 100
skills.target: I can mentally add or subtract 10 or 100 to a number from 100 to 900.
skills.misconception: Changing the wrong digit (adding 10 to the ones), or not regrouping when the tens digit is 9 (395 + 10 = 3,105).
skills.howToAddress: Use base-ten blocks: adding 10 means one more rod. Ask “Which place changed, and by how much?”

skills.name: Adding within 100
skills.target: I can add two-digit numbers within 100 using place value, and make a new ten when the ones add to 10 or more.
skills.misconception: Not making a ten from 10 or more ones (47 + 35 → 712), or adding the tens digits as ones.
skills.howToAddress: Add tens and tens, ones and ones on a place-value mat; trade ten ones for a ten before writing the sum.

skills.name: Subtracting within 100
skills.target: I can subtract within 100 using place value, breaking apart a ten when there are not enough ones.
skills.misconception: Subtracting the smaller digit from the larger digit in each place (52 − 27 → 35).
skills.howToAddress: Model with blocks: if there are not enough ones, trade one ten for ten ones first.

skills.name: Addition and Subtraction Are Related
skills.target: I can use addition to check subtraction and to find an unknown number within 100.
skills.misconception: Checking 63 − 28 = 35 by subtracting again instead of adding 35 + 28.
skills.howToAddress: Show both on one part-part-whole diagram: the parts add to the whole.

skills.name: Adding Three or Four Two-Digit Numbers
skills.target: I can add up to four two-digit numbers by adding tens and ones or by finding friendly pairs.
skills.misconception: Losing an addend, or forgetting the new tens when the ones add to 20 or more.
skills.howToAddress: Cross off each addend as it is used; add all the tens, then all the ones, then combine.

skills.name: Explaining Addition and Subtraction Strategies
skills.target: I can explain why a strategy works using place value and properties of operations.
skills.misconception: Saying a strategy works “because the answer is right” without naming tens and ones, or thinking order matters in addition.
skills.howToAddress: Use sentence frames: “I broke ___ into ___ tens and ___ ones because …”; compare two strategies side by side.

skills.name: Add To and Take From Problems
skills.target: I can solve add-to and take-from problems when the result, the change, or the start is unknown.
skills.misconception: Using key words (“more” means add) instead of the story, especially when the start is unknown.
skills.howToAddress: Act out or draw the story; mark the part that is unknown with a box, then write the equation.

skills.name: Put Together and Take Apart Problems
skills.target: I can solve put-together and take-apart problems when the total or one part is unknown.
skills.misconception: Adding the total and the known part when a part is unknown.
skills.howToAddress: Draw a part-part-whole bar model and label the whole and each part before computing.

skills.name: Compare Problems
skills.target: I can solve compare problems that ask how many more or how many fewer, or the bigger or smaller amount.
skills.misconception: Adding whenever the word “more” appears, even when the bigger amount is given.
skills.howToAddress: Draw two bars lined up; the difference is the extra part of the longer bar.

skills.name: Two-Step Word Problems
skills.target: I can solve two-step word problems within 100 and write an equation with a symbol for the unknown.
skills.misconception: Doing only the first step, or using all the numbers with one operation.
skills.howToAddress: Ask “What do I need to know first?” and write a separate equation for each step.

skills.name: Adding Three-Digit Numbers with Models
skills.target: I can add three-digit numbers with base-ten blocks or drawings by adding hundreds, tens, and ones.
skills.misconception: Adding hundreds to tens or ones (300 + 40 + 5 read as 300 + 4 + 5).
skills.howToAddress: Sort the blocks by place before combining and record each place total.

skills.name: Adding with New Tens and Hundreds
skills.target: I can add within 1,000 when I need to make a new ten or a new hundred and relate it to a written method.
skills.misconception: Writing a two-digit place total in one place (ones add to 13, so 13 is written in the ones place).
skills.howToAddress: Trade ten ones for a ten and ten tens for a hundred on the mat; record the trade in the written method.

skills.name: Subtracting Three-Digit Numbers with Models
skills.target: I can subtract three-digit numbers with base-ten blocks or drawings, or by counting up.
skills.misconception: Subtracting in the wrong order in a place (smaller minus larger digit).
skills.howToAddress: Model the first number only, then take away; or count up from the smaller number on an open number line.

skills.name: Subtracting with Regrouping
skills.target: I can subtract within 1,000 when I need to break apart a ten or a hundred, including across zeros.
skills.misconception: Not regrouping across a zero (500 − 123 → 423) or forgetting to reduce the hundred after trading.
skills.howToAddress: Show 500 as 4 hundreds, 9 tens, 10 ones with blocks before subtracting.

skills.name: Measuring with a Ruler
skills.target: I can measure the length of an object to the nearest inch or centimeter with a ruler.
skills.misconception: Starting at 1 instead of 0, or counting the tick marks instead of the spaces.
skills.howToAddress: Line up the end of the object with 0 and count the units (spaces) it covers.

skills.name: Choosing a Measuring Tool and Unit
skills.target: I can choose a ruler, yardstick, meter stick, or measuring tape and the best unit for the length I need to measure.
skills.misconception: Choosing the tool with the biggest numbers, or measuring a long hallway in centimeters with a short ruler.
skills.howToAddress: Compare how many times the tool would need to be moved; choose the tool that fits the object.

skills.name: Measuring with Different Units
skills.target: I can measure an object with two units and explain why a smaller unit gives a bigger number.
skills.misconception: Thinking a larger number always means a longer object, even when the units are different.
skills.howToAddress: Measure the same desk with paper clips and with pencils and compare the counts.

skills.name: Estimating Lengths
skills.target: I can estimate lengths in inches, feet, centimeters, and meters using benchmarks.
skills.misconception: Mixing up the size of the units (a door is 2 inches tall).
skills.howToAddress: Use body benchmarks: a fingertip is about 1 centimeter, a paper clip about 1 inch, a long step about 1 meter.

skills.name: How Much Longer?
skills.target: I can measure two objects and find how much longer one is than the other.
skills.misconception: Adding the two lengths, or comparing measurements that use different units.
skills.howToAddress: Line up the objects at 0 and find the difference by counting up from the shorter length.

skills.name: Line Plots of Measurements
skills.target: I can measure several objects to the nearest whole unit and show the data on a line plot.
skills.misconception: Putting every X at a different place, or reading the number of X marks as the length.
skills.howToAddress: Build the line plot from a tally of the measurements; each X is one object.

units.name: Length Problems and the Number Line

skills.name: Length Word Problems
skills.target: I can solve addition and subtraction word problems about lengths in the same unit.
skills.misconception: Ignoring units or combining lengths in different units, or adding when a length is cut off.
skills.howToAddress: Draw the lengths on a ruler or bar diagram and label every length with its unit.

skills.name: Whole Numbers on a Number Line
skills.target: I can show a whole number as a length from 0 on a number line with equally spaced numbers.
skills.misconception: Counting the tick marks instead of the spaces, or starting the count at 1.
skills.howToAddress: Treat the number line as a ruler: count the jumps (spaces) from 0.

skills.name: Adding and Subtracting on a Number Line
skills.target: I can show sums and differences within 100 as jumps on a number line.
skills.misconception: Jumping in the wrong direction for subtraction, or reading the jump length instead of where it lands.
skills.howToAddress: Say where you start, which way you jump, and how far before drawing the arrow.

skills.name: Telling Time to Five Minutes
skills.target: I can tell and write time to the nearest five minutes from analog and digital clocks.
skills.misconception: Reading the minute hand as the number it points to (pointing at 4 → 4 minutes), or mixing up the hour and minute hands.
skills.howToAddress: Count the minute hand by 5s around the clock; check the hour hand is just past the hour.

skills.name: AM and PM
skills.target: I can use AM and PM (a.m. and p.m.) to tell the time of day for events.
skills.misconception: Thinking AM means morning only until 10 o'clock, or that noon is AM.
skills.howToAddress: Use a daily schedule from midnight to midnight; AM is from midnight to noon; PM is from noon to midnight.

skills.name: Counting Coins
skills.target: I can find the value of a group of quarters, dimes, nickels, and pennies and write it with ¢.
skills.misconception: Counting coins by size or number (3 coins = 3¢), or thinking a nickel is worth more than a dime because it is bigger.
skills.howToAddress: Sort the coins from greatest to least value, then skip count (25s, 10s, 5s, 1s).

skills.name: Counting Bills and Coins
skills.target: I can find the value of dollar bills and coins together and write it with $ and ¢.
skills.misconception: Writing $ and ¢ in the same amount ($35¢), or adding dollars and cents as if they were the same unit.
skills.howToAddress: Count the bills first in dollars, then the coins in cents; write dollars with $ and cents with ¢.

skills.name: Money Word Problems
skills.target: I can solve word problems about money, including finding totals, change, and how much more is needed.
skills.misconception: Adding when the problem asks how much is left or how much more is needed.
skills.howToAddress: Draw the coins or a bar model of the total and the part spent, then decide which part is unknown.

skills.name: Reading Picture Graphs
skills.target: I can read a picture graph where each picture stands for 1 and tell how many are in each category.
skills.misconception: Counting pictures in the wrong row, or adding all rows when asked about one.
skills.howToAddress: Point to each picture as you count and read the label at the start of the row.

skills.name: Reading Bar Graphs
skills.target: I can read a bar graph with a scale of 1 and tell how many are in each category.
skills.misconception: Counting the grid lines instead of reading the number where the bar ends, or starting at 1.
skills.howToAddress: Slide a finger from the top of the bar straight across to the scale and read the number.

skills.name: Solving Problems with Graphs
skills.target: I can use a picture graph or bar graph to solve put-together, take-apart, and compare problems.
skills.misconception: Adding when the question asks how many more, or comparing the wrong categories.
skills.howToAddress: Write the two numbers you need from the graph first, then decide whether to add or subtract.

skills.name: Making Picture Graphs and Bar Graphs
skills.target: I can make a picture graph or bar graph from a tally chart or table with up to four categories.
skills.misconception: Making bars or rows that do not match the data, or forgetting a title, labels, or a key.
skills.howToAddress: Check each bar against the tally chart, then add the title and labels.

skills.name: Naming Shapes by Sides and Angles
skills.target: I can identify triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, and hexagons by counting their sides and angles.
skills.misconception: Naming shapes by how they look or how they are turned (a turned square is a “diamond”), or counting a vertex twice.
skills.howToAddress: Mark each side as it is counted; turn the shape and count again to see the name does not change.

skills.name: Drawing Shapes with Given Attributes
skills.target: I can draw or choose a shape that has a given number of sides, angles, or vertices.
skills.misconception: Drawing shapes with gaps or curved sides, or thinking all quadrilaterals are squares or rectangles.
skills.howToAddress: Draw on dot paper with a ruler; check the number of straight sides and corners against the description.

skills.name: Cubes and Their Faces
skills.target: I can identify a cube and describe its 6 equal square faces, edges, and vertices.
skills.misconception: Counting only the faces that can be seen in a picture, or calling any box a cube.
skills.howToAddress: Handle a real cube and mark each face with a sticker as it is counted.

skills.name: Partitioning Rectangles into Squares
skills.target: I can partition a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares and count to find how many.
skills.misconception: Drawing squares of different sizes, or counting some squares twice.
skills.howToAddress: Use square tiles first, then draw lines across and down; count by rows.

skills.name: Halves, Thirds, and Fourths
skills.target: I can partition circles and rectangles into 2, 3, or 4 equal shares and describe them as halves, thirds, or fourths.
skills.misconception: Calling unequal parts halves or thirds, or thinking more parts means bigger shares.
skills.howToAddress: Fold paper shapes to check the shares match; compare a half and a fourth of the same strip.

skills.name: Describing the Whole and Equal Shares
skills.target: I can describe a whole as two halves, three thirds, or four fourths, and explain that equal shares can have different shapes.
skills.misconception: Thinking equal shares must look the same, or that a whole is “one half and one half” only for circles.
skills.howToAddress: Cut two identical squares into halves in different ways and show the pieces cover the same amount.
